content.text:
Let me analyze the constellation data. Key pattern: for aluminium, graphite, and copper, the hotspot temperature barely changes across thicknesses 10-30mm (e.g., graphite stays ~325K, aluminium ~324K, copper ~322K) — meaning the FE hotspot is dominated by lateral spreading conductance (k×t) plus convection, not raw thickness, and it appears saturated already at 10mm. Areal mass scales with density×thickness, so the figure of merit for minimizing mass is density/conductivity: graphite (12) and aluminium (13.5) are far better than copper (22.4) or aluminium_nitride (19.2). This suggests going thinner than 10mm, especially with graphite or aluminium, could substantially cut mass while still passing the 340K hotspot requirement — until spreading resistance starts to dominate at very low thickness.

I'll screen a batch of thinner single-layer candidates to test this hypothesis before spending transport budget.

2mm graphite passes with mass 3.6 kg/m² (margin 4.69K on the tightest requirement, hotspot). This is now the lightest all-PASS design by a wide margin over everything else tested. Let me reason about whether anything lighter remains to try before spending more budget.

Graphite has the lowest density (1800 kg/m³) of every material in the table, so for any given total thickness, an all-graphite plate is the lightest possible layer stack — substituting any denser material for part of it can only add mass. We've now bracketed graphite's failure point precisely: 1mm fails (344K, over by ~4.4K), 2mm passes (335K, margin 4.69K). Since thicknesses must be whole millimetres, there is no thinner all-graphite option, and no multi-layer combination at ≤2mm total can beat plain 2mm graphite (any second material is denser than graphite). The only way to go lighter would require a material lighter than graphite with adequate conductivity — none exists in the table (epoxy is lighter but its conductivity, 0.2 W/mK, is ~750× too low to plausibly spread heat).

I'm confident further transports won't find a lighter all-PASS design, so I'll stop here and finish.

content.text:
## Final Report

**Lightest all-PASS design found: 2mm graphite, 3.6 kg/m²** — found at the 6th transport (evaluation), with hotspot 335K (4.69K margin against the 340K limit), mass 3.6 kg (96.4 kg margin), thickness 0.2 cm (3.8 cm margin). This beats the best prior-campaign result (10mm graphite at 18 kg/m², a 5× mass reduction).

**How I got there:** The constellation showed hotspot temperature was nearly flat (322–325K) across 10–30mm thicknesses for aluminium, graphite, and copper, suggesting the FE hotspot was saturated by lateral spreading rather than through-thickness conduction — implying much thinner plates might still pass. Testing thin single-layer candidates confirmed this: 1mm graphite failed (344K), but 2mm graphite passed (335K). Graphite has the lowest density (1800 kg/m³) of every material in the table, so no substitution or multi-layer combination at ≤2mm total thickness could beat it on mass. I also cross-checked aluminium and copper at similar thicknesses (both passed but weighed more: 5.4 and 8.96 kg/m² respectively), confirming graphite dominates.

**Why I stopped at 7/12 transports:** Since thicknesses must be whole millimetres and graphite (the lowest-density viable conductor) already fails at 1mm, there is no thinner all-graphite option, and every other material is denser, so no combination at ≤2mm total can weigh less. Epoxy is lighter (1200 kg/m³) but its conductivity (0.2 W/mK) is roughly 750× too low to plausibly spread the heat flux, so it wasn't worth spending budget to confirm.

**What I'd try with more budget:** Test whether a very thin asymmetric two-material stack (e.g., a sub-millimetre-equivalent high-conductivity cap) could ever be legal under whole-mm constraints in a way I haven't considered, or explore non-uniform designs Core's model doesn't currently accept — but under the current whole-mm, isotropic-material constraints, I believe 2mm graphite is the true optimum in this arm's search space.
